benchmark_details.name: Blacklist Cards
benchmark_details.overview: Tests models on extracting company, location, identification number, stamped date and the blacklist entries from mostly typewritten index cards of the Swiss Federal Archives on Swiss firms and individuals put on the British trade blacklist in 1940–1946.

purpose_and_intended_users.goal: Measure how well vision-language models extract the fields of a uniform, mostly typewritten index card into a structured record: separating company name from location, reading the identification number, normalising a stamped date, and transcribing the text blocks that record when a firm was put on and taken off the British blacklist. The results serve researchers and developers comparing models on archival index cards, and practitioners in archives, historical research and digital humanities projects who choose a model for digitising large series of uniform cards.
tasks: field extraction from index card images
transcription of typed and handwritten text blocks
purpose_and_intended_users.limitations:
The 33 cards come from one record series of one archive and all follow the same layout; results do not transfer to other card types. The ground truth was drafted by a model and corrected by hand (see Annotation), so where a card is ambiguous it may lean towards that model's reading. The split of company and location and the omitted commas and periods follow the annotators' conventions rather than a published standard.

Blocks in `information` are compared by position (see Calculation), so a merged, split or reordered block lowers the score of every block after it, while blocks beyond those in the ground truth cost nothing. Empty fields are scored too: 27 of 33 cards have no stamped date, and a response that also leaves `date` empty gets full marks for it, so an all-empty response already scores about 0.15.
out_of_scope_uses: drawing conclusions about the firms or persons named on the cards
evaluating handwriting recognition on free-form documents

data.source: Index cards from the Swiss Federal Archives (Schweizerisches Bundesarchiv), signature E2001E#1968/78#7508*: https://www.recherche.bar.admin.ch/recherche/#/de/archiv/einheit/31240458. The record documents Swiss firms and individuals put on the British trade blacklist during the Second World War; it comprises over 1,000 cards. Each card gives the name and location in the top left, an identification number (`B.51.322.GB.…`) in the top right, and in the body the amendment of the blacklist that added the entry and the one that removed it ("gestrichen"), sometimes with notes on the French list.
data.annotation: A model drafted the ground truth by running the benchmark with the `Card` dataclass, most likely one of the two models configured when the benchmark was added, Gemini 2.5 Flash (preview) or GPT-4.1; which one is not recorded. Lea Kasper and Sorin Marti then reviewed and corrected every card by hand. Commas after names and periods after locations are omitted. Dates in `information` are transcribed, not normalised.
data.collection_date: Source documents: blacklist amendments of 1940–1946, recorded in an index created 1946–1948. Added to the benchmark: October 2025.
data.contamination_controls: None. The card images, prompt and ground truth have been public in this repository since October 2025.

methods: zero-shot structured extraction from a single image per request
structured JSON output requested using the `Card` dataclass
one prompt, [prompt.txt](prompts/prompt.txt), used by all tests
temperature 0.5 in all tests, overridden or omitted for some models in `scripts/benchmark_base.py`
output cap: the repository default of 16,384 tokens per request, adjusted per model in `scripts/benchmark_base.py`
methodology.calculation:
Every terminal field of the ground truth (for example `company.transcription` or `information[1].transcription`) is looked up at the same path in the response. Fields only in the response are ignored. `None` and the string `"null"` are treated as empty strings on both sides.

- identical values score 1.0, including two empty strings
- otherwise the score is the rapidfuzz `ratio` divided by 100, between 0 and 1; there is no threshold, and an empty value against a non-empty one scores 0

The card score is the mean over that card's fields. The benchmark score is the mean of the card scores. A response that cannot be parsed into the schema is not scored and does not enter the mean.
methodology.interpretation: Scores range from 0 to 1; higher is better. Partial string similarity earns partial credit, so small slips (a missing period in the identification number) cost little. A score near 0.15 is no better than an empty response (see Baseline Results).
methodology.baseline_results:
Model results are available on the [benchmark page](https://rise-services.rise.unibas.ch/benchmarks/p/benchmarks/blacklist_cards) and in `results/<date>/<test_id>/` at the repository root. Compare runs with the same prompt, scoring rules and ground-truth revision, and report the number of successfully scored objects alongside the score. No fixed baseline run is designated. As a scorer diagnostic, an empty parsed object scores 0.153535 on the 33 ground-truth files, because missing values are normalised to empty strings; it is not a schema-valid model response.

Observed across models: models separate company name and location, extract the identification number and transcribe the two dated lines reliably. Dates in the text blocks stay as written; turning them into structured dates for analysis is left to a later processing step.
methodology.validation: The annotators reviewed and corrected every ground-truth file by hand after the model draft. Scoring is deterministic; the scorer is covered by the repository's test suite.
methodology.validity_justification: Field-level similarity reflects the downstream use: each card becomes a database record, and near-misses need less correction than wrong values.

ethical_and_legal_considerations.privacy_and_anonymity: The cards name the firms and, on 13 of the 33 cards, individuals (some with business addresses) who were placed on the British blacklist in 1940–1946. They are not anonymised. Firms are not natural persons. The cards give no birth dates, but anyone economically active in 1940–1946 was very likely born before 1926 and would be at least 100 years old in 2026. The Swiss Federal Archives have made the record freely accessible since 1978.
ethical_and_legal_considerations.data_licensing: Source material: Public Domain. Ground truth, prompts and other data created for this benchmark: CC BY 4.0.
ethical_and_legal_considerations.compliance_with_regulations: The cards are federal archival records held by the Swiss Federal Archives and fall under the Federal Act on Archiving (BGA, SR 152.1). The archive's record assigns them the ordinary protection period of 30 years (Art. 9 para. 1 BGA), which ended in 1978; no extended protection for personal data applies. As official records they carry no copyright and are used as public domain. No ethical review was carried out.
